title: Bellman-Ford
tagline: Shortest paths that tolerate negative edges — and detect negative cycles.

intuition.analogy: Rumours spreading through an office: after one round everyone one desk away knows; after two rounds, two desks away. After V−1 rounds, the news has had time to travel the longest possible simple path to everyone.
paragraphs: Dijkstra's greedy choice fails with negative edges. Bellman-Ford instead brute-forces correctness: it relaxes every edge repeatedly. After k rounds, all shortest paths using at most k edges are correct.
A shortest path in a graph with V vertices uses at most V−1 edges, so V−1 rounds of relaxing all edges settles every distance.

Bonus: if a V-th round still improves some distance, a negative-weight cycle exists (reachable from the source). That detection ability is unique and valuable — e.g. arbitrage detection in currency graphs.
intuition.keyIdea: Relax all edges V−1 times; one more improving round signals a negative cycle.

steps.title: Relax V−1 times
steps.detail: Repeat V−1 rounds; in each, for every edge (u,v,w): if dist[u]+w < dist[v], update dist[v].

steps.title: Detect negative cycles
steps.detail: Run one extra round. Any edge that still relaxes proves a reachable negative cycle.

pitfalls: Skip edges from unreached nodes (dist == ∞) to avoid spurious updates.
It's much slower than Dijkstra — only use it when negatives or cycle detection are needed.
Negative-cycle detection only catches cycles reachable from the source.

rows: B=4, C=2, then C→B makes B=-1, D=1
dryRun.clickMoment: The negative edge C→B pulls B's distance below its direct value. Dijkstra would have already finalised B at 4 and missed this — repeated relaxation is what saves Bellman-Ford.
